claims.text: Hot-rolling followed by controlled annealing can produce a bimodal grain-size distribution in structural high-entropy alloys.
A bimodal grain-size distribution will improve strength relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
A bimodal grain-size distribution will improve ductility relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
A bimodal grain-size distribution will improve Young's modulus relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
A bimodal grain-size distribution will improve fracture resistance relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
Fine grains increase yield strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Coarse grains reduce strain localization and thereby enhance ductility.
Coarse grains enhance energy absorption during crack propagation and improve fracture toughness.
The controlled thermal treatment minimizes deleterious precipitate formation.
Minimizing deleterious precipitate formation preserves or slightly improves Young's modulus.
The treatment is expected to increase yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to homogeneous HEA microstructures.
The treatment is expected to enhance ductility by approximately 5–10% relative to homogeneous HEA microstructures.
The treatment is expected to produce a measurable increase in fracture toughness.
Young's modulus is expected to remain comparable to or be modestly higher than that of homogeneous HEA microstructures.
The proposed benefits depend on controlled thermal gradients and predictable bimodal-grain formation.
Rapid grain growth at elevated temperatures can eliminate the bimodal structure and negate its mechanical benefits.
The approach may fail for HEA compositions that respond poorly to thermomechanical processing or when process parameters are inadequately controlled.
SEM or EBSD can be used to determine whether the treated material has a bimodal grain-size distribution.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says Young's modulus will improve, whereas the predicted outcome allows it merely to remain comparable.

The hypothesis requires simultaneous improvement in four properties, but the falsification rule requires statistically significant improvement in only two; therefore, failure to improve one or two of the four properties would contradict the hypothesis without necessarily falsifying it under the stated rule.
